I N T R O D U C T I ON
 
I,  the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee  on Industry,  having   been   authorized 
by the  Committee, hereby present this   182
nd Report on the Action Taken by the Government on the recommendations
contained in the Committee’160th Report Tax Proposals Affecting the Various Segments of Industries (Ministry of
Small Scale Industries).
2. The Committee examined and considered the Action Taken Notes supplied by the Ministry of Small Scale Industries
on the recommendations contained 160th   Report on Tax proposals Affecting the Various Segments of Industries
(Ministry of Small Scale Industries). This report is based on the outcome of such examination. 
3. The Committee in its meeting held on 16
TH May, 2006 considered and adopted the Report.
 
NEW DELHI;
16
TH May, 2006
SANTOSH BAGRODIA
Chairman Department -related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Industry
 
                                   
REPORT
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Small Scale Industries on
the Recommendations contained in the  160th      Report (of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
on Industry) On Tax Proposals Affecting The Various Segments Of Industries pertaining to (Ministry Of Small Scale
Industries). The Report was presented /laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha on  the 5
th May, 2005.
 
2.         Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Small Scale Industries     in respect of the  
recommendations contained in the Report.   These have been categorized as follows:
 
Chapter - I- The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry :- Paras :  2.23 , 2.45 , 3.19,
3.22 and 3.23
 
             The Committee is pleased to observe that  the   Ministry  has accepted its  recommendation as  mentioned in
Chapter –I of the  Report.

Chapter - II- The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the
Government's replies: - Paras :-  2.9, 2.18 and 2.38 .
 
 In respect of these recommendations the Committee is  convinced  with the logic and explanation  advocated by the
Ministry  and therefore   does not want to  pursue  further. 
 
Chapter - III- The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee has not accepted replies of the
Ministry Paras:-  1.14 , 2.2, 2.11 , 2.14 , 2.15, 2.42 , 2.50,  3.3 , 3.8  and  3.11
 
 The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementation  of recommendations contained in  Chapter-III  and
desires that the Ministry should furnish  logical  explanation  in respect of these recommendations.  
 
Chapter - IV- The recommendations/observations in respect of which  final replies of the  Ministry have not been
received :- Paras:-  3.12, 3.13 , 3.16
 
In respect  of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV, the Ministry has  either   furnished the interim replies or couched
its language in  vague terms like  noted for compliance/guidance, therefore, the Committee desires  that the Ministry
should furnish Action Taken Notes in  respects of recommendations categorized   in Chapter-IV  in detail and to the
point, as per the intention and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee.
                                   
3.         The Details of the ATR is being discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.
CHAPTER - I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
1.0       Withdrawal of CVD exemption on raw materials for manufacture of blades for rotors of wind operated
electricity generators
1.1       The Committee directs the Government to look into the matter of withdrawal of CVD exemption on raw
materials for manufacture of blades for rotors of wind operated electricity generators and ensure that the industry is not
affected adversely
 
(Para 2.23 )
ACTION TAKEN
 
1.1.1    The Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance has informed that the issue was examined in consultation with
Ministry of Non Conventional Energy Sources and CVD exemption on 15 specified raw materials for the manufacture
of rotor blades of wind operated energy generators has already been granted.
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
1.2       Vocational institutes and recreational training
 
1.2.1    The Committee is of the view that the Department of Revenue should give kind consideration to exempt the
vocational institutes and recreational training institute including the institutes under philanthropic non-profit making
organizations from the Service Tax.  
(Para 2.45 )
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
 1.2.2   At present, service tax is levied on commercial training or coaching provided to any person by a commercial
training or coaching centers. Service tax is levied on the gross amount charged for rendering taxable service. No service
tax is leviable, if the taxable service is rendered without charging any amount from the recipient.
1.2.3    However, such commercial coaching or training provided by vocational training institutes and recreational
training institutes are presently exempt vide Notification No. 24/2004 - Service Tax, dated 10.9.2004.

RECOMMENDATIONS
 
1.3       Early Harvest Scheme India-Thailand FTA
 
1.3.1    The Department of Revenue may re-consider the reduction of customs duties on inputs (up to 5%) required to
manufacture   products covered in Early Harvest Scheme India-Thailand FTA.(Para 3.19)
 
ACTION TAKEN
1.3.2    Vide notification No.27/2004-Cus dated 23.01.2004, concessional rate of duty has already been prescribed on a
number of inputs required for the manufacture of goods covered under the India-Thailand Early Harvesting Scheme.
 
RECOMMENDATION
1.4       Duty rates of 5% , 8% and 10%
1.4.1    The Committee desires that the Department of Revenue may facilitate the industries with its declared item wise
time frame for achieving duty rates of 5% , 8% and 10% as recommended by (FRBM)  task force headed by Dr. Vijay
Kelkar so that various segments of industries in general would accordingly chalk out their short term and long term
business strategy.                  (Para 3.22)
 
ACTION TAKEN
1.4.2    It is the declared policy of the Government to bring the customs duty structure closer to that of our East Asian
neighbours. In line with this policy, the peak rate of customs duty on non-agricultural goods (with a few exception) has
been reduced to 15%. Simultaneously, to further improve the competitiveness of domestic industry and to reduce costs,
customs duty on specified basic raw materials such as crude petroleum oil, specified chemicals, specified polymers,
primary iron and steel, etc., has been reduced to 5% or 10%.
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
1.5       Continuation of 8% SED on car and aerated waters
 
1.5.1    While the Committee is in agreement with withdrawal of 8% SED on a number of items like tyre, tubes, flaps
and polyster, filament yarn and even air conditioner, however, the Committee would like to know the reasons for
continuation of 8% SED on car and aerated waters.  (Para 3.23 )
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
1.5.2    It is the intention of the Government to bring as many goods as possible to the Cenvat rate of 16%. With this end
in view, the 8% SED was withdrawn on tyres, polyester filament yarn and air-conditioners. Because of revenue
considerations, it was not possible to abolish the SED on all items. The Finance Minister in his Budget speech has
indicated that manufacturers of motorcars and aerated drinks would have to wait for some more time.
CHAPTER - II
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO
PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT'S REPLIES
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
2.0       Excise duty on synthetic and artificial staple fibers
 
2.1.1    The Committee, urges upon the Government that the excise duty on synthetic and artificial staple fibres under
Chapter Heading 55.03& 55.04 of Central Excise Tariff may be reduced to 8% in this Budget itself.
(Para 2.9 )
ACTION TAKEN
 
2.1.2    The issue was taken up with the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance. They have informed that in 2004

182nd Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/182ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 13:00:50]
budget, Government had rationalized the duty structure for textile sector.  So far as cotton is concerned, there are two
options. Under the first option, there is exemption right from the fibre to the garment stage.  For those units who want to
avail of credit of duty paid on inputs/capital goods and of service tax, an alternative option to pay duty at 4% was given.
So far as man-made and synthetic sector is concerned, there is a mandatory duty only at the first point
 i.e. fibre/filament
yarn stage. Beyond this stage, two options are available. Downstream manufacturers of spun yarn, fabrics, garment can
opt for full exemption. Under the other option, those who want to pay duty, 8% duty has been prescribed as against 16%
earlier. A lower duty of 8% on spun yarn and fabrics was proposed so that there was an incentive to the manufacturers
to opt for the Cenvat stream.   
 
2.1.3    Various stages in the manufacture of polyester fibres are as under:
Naphtha (16%)            Paraxylene  (16%)        DMT/PTA (16%)         Polyester Fibre (16%)
(Figures in brackets represent the rate of excise duty)
2.1.4    If excise duty on polyester fibre is reduced to 8%, the problem of inversion will shift tothe fibre manufacturers,
as in their case, the finished products will attract duty at 8%, while the raw materials would be paying 16%. Therefore,
if 8% rate has to be achieved on polyester fibre, excise duty has to be reduced down the line on all the raw materials
starting from Naphtha. This would involve a very substantial revenue loss.
2.1.5    It has been ascertained that some manufacturers of yarn are opting to pay duty and accumulating credit, hoping
to utilize the same later on or get a refund of the same in case of exports.   If a yarn manufacturer faces a problem of
excess credit by opting for the route of 8% rate, there is noting to prevent him to switch over to exemption route. If the
problem is one of excess credit, then the solution would lie in raising the optional excise duty to 16% as that would
obviate all problems of inversion. The suggestion to reduce the duty to 8% will also go against the policy of moving
towards a mean cenvat rate of 16%.  For a unit opting for the exemption route, with a single stage duty on a garment is
about 4% - 5% of the retail price of the garment, which cannot be considered as excessive.  Under the circumstances, it
is felt there is no case for reducing the mandatory duty of 16% on fibres.     
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
2.2.                  Duty differential of 5% between the finished product (PVC) and feedstock (VCM)
 
2.2.1    The Committee is an agreement with the argument of the representative of the industries that the present duty
differential of 5% between the finished product (PVC) and feedstock (VCM) is insufficient to cover even the variable
costs and is therefore not only detrimental to the growth of the industry but also threatening its very viability. Therefore,
The Committee desires that the Department of Revenue should reconsider to reduce the import duty on VCM to 0%
from the current level of 5% and roll back the import duty on finished product PVC resin to the earlier level of 15%.
(Para 2.18 )
ACTION TAKEN
 
2.2.2 Prior to 1.3.2005, Poly Vinyl Chloride (PVC) attracted customs duty of 15%, while Vinyl Chloride Monomer
(VCM) attracted duty of 10%. There was thus a duty differential of 5% between PVC and VCM.
 
2.2.3  Polymers are basic raw material and, in this year’s budget, customs duty on certain specified polymers including
PVC was reduced from 15% to 10%.  Simultaneously in order to maintain 5% duty differential between PVC and VCM,
duty on VCM was also reduced from 10% to 5%.  In a low customs duty regime, it would generally not be possible to
maintain a duty differential of more than 5% between feedstock and finished products.
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
2.3       Excise duties exemption to SSI
 
2.3.1    The Committee pleads that even to the Department of Revenue the Kelkar Committee's recommendation on
confining the excise duties exemption to SSI to a limit of 40 lakh is not acceptable, and there is a valid reason for non
acceptance of the Kelker Committee's recommendations on the issue keeping in view the inflation rate and largely the
reasons on account of the need for giving adequate space to small enterprises to grow into medium enterprises as per the
declared policy of the Government.Therefore, there is the need for purposive and supportive tax structure   to give flip

to emerging SMEs.  The Committee understands that there is the strong reason for enhancing the excise duties
exemption to SSI from the current level to a reasonable level.
(Para 2.38 )
ACTION TAKEN
 
2.3.2    The Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance has mentioned that the number of SSI units paying central
excise duty is about 37,000, which contribute only about 2.57% of the total revenue from central excise duties. SSI
exemption, thus, adversely affects the tax-GDP ratio. Excise duty being a tax at the manufacturing stage (the first stage),
exemption from it also leads to non-accounting of production, which in turn leads to non-payment of other taxes, such
as income tax, sales tax, etc. and generation of black money. Such exemption also leads to misuse of CENVAT credit
by large duty-paying units against duty-paid documents for materials supplied to the exempted SSI sector. It also results
in breaking of the CENVAT chain. State-level Value Added Tax (VAT) has been implemented from 1
st April 2005. 
Grant of more exemptions would adversely affect effective implementation of VAT. In view of the above-mentioned
facts, the Ministry of Finance has informed that it would not be possible to accede to the suggestion.
CHAPTER - III
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE COMMITTEE HAS NOT
ACCEPTED REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT OR THE COMMITTEE WANTS TO MAKE FURTHER
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
3.0       Level playing field to the domestic industry
 
3.1.1    The Committee understands that the tempest of globalisation would also gallop the Temple of Modern India
unless and until level playing field is provided to the domestic industry.  Therefore, the Committee is of the strong view
that the architect of Modern India should not forget to have the protected layer of extending certain tax
concessions/exemptions to protect against the onslaught of Faustian MNCs.  (Para 1.14 )
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.1.2    The General SSI Exemption Scheme provides full exemption from excise duty for first clearances of Rs.1 crore,
if no input tax credit is availed. On clearances beyond Rs.1 crore, the unit has to pay normal duty and take CENVAT
credit on inputs. The turnover eligibility limit for availing the benefit under the Scheme has been raised from Rs.3 crore
to Rs.4 crore in the Budget 2005-06.
 
3.1.3    Further, the Income Tax Act provides a variety of fiscal incentives for promoting the industrial sector and
facilitating exports, which are also available to the small-scale industries. The Act provides for a 100% deduction of
export profits of 100% Export Oriented Units (EOUs) engaged in the manufacture or production of any article, thing or
computer software under section 10B and of units engaged in the export of wood-based handicrafts under Section
10BA, upto assessment year 2009-10. In addition, a 10-year tax benefit is provided under Section 10A of the Act to
units in Special Economic Zones (SEZs).
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.1.4    The Committee notes that the Government is extending a variety of fiscal incentives for promoting the Small
Scale Industries, however, this Committee feels that the Advisory Committee, constituted under the Chairmanship of
Member (Central Excise), Central Board of Excise and Custom (CBEC) to  advise the Government on the extent of
abatement for both excise and Service Tex, should also examine the issue of the requisite period for which such fiscal
incentive is required to promote the SSI  units. The said Advisory committee may also examine the issue of extending
the central fiscal incentives to SSI units engaged in the SSI activities to the select region of the country in such a way
that it  must ensure the balanced industrial distribution and development and prevent the shifting of the industries from
one region to another due to aberration  in the tax-incentives.

3.1,5    The Committee observes that  since the Medium enterprises are being emerging out of the SSI units and they are
on the move towards the consolidation stage, therefore, the Advisory Committee may also consider the issue of
examining  as to whether the emerging MEs require central fiscal incentives for the rapid promotion and proliferation
and catching up the global pace of growth.
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
3.2       Advisory Committee on the extent of abatement of excise duty and Service Tax
 
3.2.1    The Committee welcomes the move for setting up of Advisory Committee to advise the Government on the
extent of abatement of excise duty and Service Tax.  However, the Committee desires that the Advisory Committee
must have the representatives from various sections of economy including various segments of industry as well as
Federations/ Associations from Industries so that any conclusion could be drawn only after consultation and mutual
understanding in the general interest of the industry. (Para 2.2 )
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.2.2    Advisory Committee to advise the Government on the extent of abatement for both excise duty and service tax
has been constituted under the chairmanship of Member (Central Excise), Central Board of Excise and Customs
(CBEC). Member (Service Tax), CBEC, Additional Chief Advisor (Cost), Department of Expenditure, and Joint
Secretary (Tax Research Unit) are the members of the Committee. It has also been provided for the Committee to co-opt
any other officials of Government of India and invite experts and concerned representatives of trade and industry as
special invitees depending upon the need.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.2.3    The Committee recommends that Advisory Committee (to  advise the Government on the extent of abatement
for both excise duty and service tax) should have stake-holders as Members than merely associating them  as Special 
Invitees, that  too,  depending upon the need as felt by the Government. It would provide much more opportunity in
addressing their grievances and make the them feel of a participation in the decision-making process. It is being
observed that need is much  more felt on the part of  the stake-holders then the regulator. Moreover, the Committee feels
that the Government apparatus has to play not only the role of regulator but also that of a facilitator, therefore,
encouraging the stake-holders to participate in the decision-making process on equal footing would provide the example
of good governance. 
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
3.3       Electronic Consumer Products
 
3.3.1    The Committee understands that the market of consumer electronics is rapidly growing.  The electronic
components are the input products and back bone of electronic consumer products.  Even then no growth is coming in
the manufacture of electronic components because it cannot compete with the rapidly growing grey market due to
highest rate of excise duty @ 16%. The Committee, therefore, feels that the excise duty may be reduce to 8% for all
locally manufactured electronics products and inputs.(Para 2.11 )
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
Manufacturers of electronic goods can avail of CENVAT credit of excise duty paid on electronic
components/inputs/consumables. The actual impact of excise duties on electronic goods is less than 16%.
 
The revenue implication of reduction of excise duty/CVD on electronic components from 16% to 8% will be substantial
(over Rs.1000 crore approximately).
 
3.3.4    Reduction in excise duty from 16% to 8% would go against the stated policy of the Government that, as far as
possible, manufactured items should attract the mean CENVAT rate of 16%.

FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.3.5    The Committee impresses upon the Government to review the Policy which has been referred to  in their replies
so as to favourably  accommodate the electronic consumer products.
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
3.4       Import duty on the raw materials
 
3.4.1    The Committee wishes to point out an accepted policy of the Government that the import duty on the raw
materials has got to be lower than the duty on the finished products. Even in the world-class plants like Reliance, IPCL,
GAIL, Haldia, Finolex etc. the duty differential between the raw material and the end product is maintained.     
                                                                                                                    
(Para 2.14  )
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.4.2    The policy of the Government, in general, has been to obviate any inverted customs duty.  However, it may not
be feasible to remove the inverted duty structure in all cases, on account of various reasons such as the output of one
industry being the input of another industry, etc.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.4.3    The Committee understands the need for obviating the inverted customs duty in order to maintain the differential
duty-structure on the raw-materials and the finished products. The Committee is in agreement with the reply of the
Government that the output of one Industry may be the input of another industry therefore, it may not be possible to
remove the duty-structure in all cases. However, the Committee is of the view that tax-structure can not be on the
random basis, it has to be based on certain reasons and principles that  distinctly identifying products are the finished
products and from those which can be used still as raw - material. Such identification and its classification has to  be on
rational basis to avoid the double-taxation and to maintain the accepted general principle of taxable that the import duty
on the raw-material has got to be lower then the duty structure on the finished products. The committee’s concern is
that  the end-users should  get the solace from the rational duty structure.  and Government would also not be under any
revenue loss from the intermediate user of products which still remains as the raw materials.
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
3.5       Policies of the Government at least at par with the Large Scale Sector
 
3.5.1    In accordance with the announced policies of the Government at least at par with the Large Scale Sector, which
are at present, being rather penalized:-
 
Allow the import of DOP (HS Code 29173920 & 29173200) DBP (HS Code 19173910 & 29173100) only from the
Exporters who qualify the Indian norms of S.S.I.Units.
AND/OR
Restore fair competition by subjecting DOP and DBP to a higher rate of customs duty in cases where the exporters do
not qualify as SSI units as per Indian Regulations. Such imports may be subjected to duty at the bound rate of 40%.  It is
submitted that such a course of action will be compatible with the WTO Article III on national treatment.
 
Provide a 10% duty differential between raw material to end products. The custom duty on its  Raw Material (HS
Code), Octanol/2 Ethyl Hexannol (29051600&29051620, Butanol (Iso/Normal?mixed) 29051300& 29051400, Iso
Nonanol/Other (29051900), Phthalic Anhydride (29173500)
(Para  2.15)
 

182nd Report of Committee on Industry

ACTION TAKEN
 
3.3.2    The Committee was apprised fo the following action taken by the government:-
 
Customs duty on DOP and DBP is 15%.  Duty on their raw material is 15%. Thus, there is no anomaly in the duty
structure.
Providing differentiated duty structure depending on the status of exporter would complicate the duty structure and be
administratively difficult to implement.
With a peak customs duty of 15%, it may not always be possible to provide a duty differential of 10% between raw
materials and final products, in all cases. 
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.5.3    The Committee desires that SSI units should be given preferential treatment so far the duty structure is
concerned in order to promote them in the international market. Particularly, such preferential treatment may be allowed
where there remains the scope for maintaining the DOP and DBP to higher rate upto bound rate of 40% which is also
compatible to the WTO-provision. The Committee further desires that the duty differential between raw-material to end 
products has to be maintained for the sake of regulating the market-mechanics and restoration of fair competition.
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
3.6       Paint & Coating Industry
 
3.6.1    The Committee understands the problems being faced by the industry and therefore, is in agreement that the
exemption limit be reasonably raised and the restoration of concessional rate of 60% duty with the CENVAT up to
Rs.1.00 crore,  as such fiscal measures would help  in reducing the cost of SSI products and  imbibe competitive
resilience in the units engaged in Paint & Coating Industry.  (Para 2.42 )
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.6.2    Prior to 1
st April 2005,there were two separate schemes of excise duty exemption for SSI units:
Scheme I - This scheme provided full exemption from excise duty for first clearances of Rs.1 crore, if no input tax credit
is availed.   On clearances beyond Rs. 1 crore, unit was to pay normal duty.  (Notification no. 8/2003- Central Excise
dated 1st March 2003).
Scheme II - This option provided a concessional rate of excise duty of 60% of normal rate, for first clearances of Rs.1
crore, if input tax credit is availed. On clearances beyond Rs. 1 crore, unit was to pay normal duty.  (Notification no.
9/2003 - Central Excise dated 1st March 2003.)
3.6.3    In the context of excise duty exemption for SSI, the clearance limit of Rs.1 crore is referred to as ‘exemption
limit’.  In both the above schemes, exemption/concession was available only if total value of clearances of a unit in the
preceding financial year did not exceed Rs. 3 crore. This clearance limit of Rs.3 crore during the previous year is
referred to as ‘eligibility limit’
3.6.4    Before the presentation of this year’s budget, representations/recommendations were received from trade and
industry, Ministry of Small Scale Industries and VIPs seeking changes in the SSI excise duty exemption scheme, which
inter alia suggested:
Increase in exemption limit for SSI from Rs. 1 crore to Rs. 2 crore.
Increase in eligibility limit for SSI from Rs. 3 crore to 5 crore.
3.6.5    A number of Committees have looked into the scheme of exemption for the SSI units, and suggested
modifications.
3.6.6    Shome Committee on ‘ Tax Policy and Tax Administration for the Tenth Plan’ had noted that the Scheme II,
which provided for a concessional rate of 60% of normal rate with Cenvat credit, did result in a kind of subsidy due to
accumulation of credit and gave a higher benefit than the other scheme. In this background, the Committee had
recommended that:
There should not be any concessional rate of duty for SSI units for SSI units availing input credit. They should be at par

with any non-SSI unit;
or
(b)        The concessional rate of duty for Scheme II should be so adjusted that when the clearances reach Rs.1 crore the
input credit is more or less exhausted;
or
(c)     The accumulated credit should be allowed to lapse as soon as the clearances cross Rs.1 crore in a financial year.
Task Force on Indirect Taxes headed by Dr. Kelkar had, inter alia, recommended that:
SSI exemption should be extended only to small units with a turnover of Rs.50 lakh, and
Duty exemption limit for SSI should be gradually brought down to Rs.50 lakh.
3.6.7    Task Force on implementation of FRBM Act, 2003 had also examined the issue of excise duty exemption for
SSI and its implications on the economy as a whole, and recommended that:
The exemption limit for SSI should be reduced from Rs.1 crore to Rs.40 lakh;
In respect of clearances between Rs.40 lakh and Rs.1 crore, a SSI unit should have option to pay tax @ 4% without
Cenvat credit or normal rate of duty with Cenvat credit.
3.6.8 In the above background, a comprehensive review of SSI exemption schemes was undertaken in this year’s budget
and it was felt that there should not be any extra benefit for a unit opting to pay at a concessional rate of 60% of the
normal rate.  Such a scheme results in accumulation of credit, which is then used for paying duty on goods beyond the
clearances of Rs.1 crore. As a result, there is great temptation for SSI units to show a lower value addition in respect of
clearances up to Rs.1 crore. Having regard to the Shome Committee’s recommendations and the report of Task Force
FRBM, it was decided to withdraw the second scheme. Thus,                        
Second scheme of exemption, which provided for a concessional rate of 60% of normal rate with Cenvat credit up to
clearances of Rs.1 crore was withdrawn. (Such units, in any case, can opt for the full exemption up to Rs.1 crore or pay
duty from the first clearance in case they want to pass on the credit to their buyers).
The eligibility limit for SSI exemption was increased from Rs.3 crore to Rs.4 crore, because it was felt that this would
encourage a SSI unit to expand.
Though the various Task Forces had recommended reduction in exemption limit below Rs.1 crore, it was felt that this
recommendation may not be accepted, and the exemption limit of Rs.1 crore may continue, though it need not be raised.
           
         In view of the above, no change is called for in the present scheme of exemption for SSI units.     
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
           
3.6.9    The Committee is in agreement with the Ministry  for not accepting the recommendation of  Task Force for
reducing the exemption-limit below Rs.1 crore, which in fact needs to be raised keeping in view the  general inflation
and  need for giving adequate space to SEs to grow into MEs, which is a proclaimed policy of the Ministry of finance,
itself./
 
3.6.10  The Committee is in agreement with the Ministry for raising the eligibility limit for SSI exemption from Rs.3
crore to Rs.4 crore which would certainly lead to expansion of SSI units.

3.7       Fiscal Measures for a SSI-friendly tax regime
 
 3.7.1   The Committee recommends that in order to promote the small enterprises sector, certain fiscal measures need to
be taken to establish a SSI-friendly tax regime.  These include:
 
3.7.1    Extension of General SSI Excise Exemption to SSI units manufacturing branded goods in urban areas, as
available in rural areas;                                                                                        (Para  2.50)
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.7.2    The matter was taken up with the Ministry of Finance, which has informed that to check misuse of SSI
exemption by multinationals, it was provided that the SSI exemption would not be available to units manufacturing

FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.7.3    The Committee is of the view that SSI units manufacturing branded goods in Urban areas cannot be debarred
from the benefits of General SSI Exemption which is being extended to SSI units in rural areas merely on the ground to
check misuse of SSI exemption by multinationals as the same would amount to the assumption that multinationals have
not made dent to the rural areas i.e. an assumption which is too presumptuous. Moreover, misuse as such can be
checked by placing efficient and good tax-governance for the sake of tax-collection rather than debarring the Urban SSI
units from availing the Central Excise exemption. Dividing the rural and urban areas for extending SSI exemption to
SSI units would amount to differential treatment and unreasonable classification, therefore, the Committee recommends
that General SSI Excise Exemptin to SSI Units manufacturing branded goods must be `general’ and not on illogical
classification of rural or urban areas, therefore, the same be also extended to urban areas as now being extended to the
rural areas.
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
3.7.4    Increase in the excise exemption to new as well as existing SSI units in rural as well as urban areas;
(Para  2.50)(ii)
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.7.5    Ministry of Finance has mentioned that the number of SSI units paying central excise duty is about 37,000,
which contribute only about 2.57% of the total revenue from central excise duties.  SSI exemption, thus, adversely
affects the tax-GDP ratio. Excise duty being a tax at the manufacturing stage (the first stage), exemption from it also
leads to non-accounting of production, which in turn leads to non-payment of other taxes, such as income tax, sales tax,
etc. and generation of black money. Such exemption also leads to misuse of CENVAT credit by large duty-paying units
against duty-paid documents for materials supplied to the exempted SSI sector. It also results in breaking of the
CENVAT chain. State-level Value Added Tax (VAT) has been implemented from 1
st April 2005. Grant of more
exemptions would adversely affect effective implementation of VAT. In view of the above-mentioned facts, Ministry of
Finance has informed that it would not be possible to accede to these suggestions.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.7.6    The Committee reiterates its recommendation for increase inn the Excise exemption to new as well as  existing
SSI units in rural as well as the urban areas and urges the Government to have a favorable view in the matter.

RECOMMENDATIONS
 
3.8       Lowering the customs and increasing the excise duty
 
3.8.1    The Committee views that current regime of lowering the customs and increasing the excise duty on items like
steel will have serious implications for the PSEs in capital goods sector. The Committee cautions the Government that
such a Duty regime would result in an uneven competition with PSEs facing serious handicap against cheaper imports
and MNCs. If the Government is serious about reviving the PSEs, it must help them regain their standing in domestic
market instead of imposing a duty regime that perpetuates the disadvantage against cheap imports. It is the
responsibility of the Government to seek redressal, if necessary, against such an uneven competition under the WTO
provisions.(Para  3.3)
ACTION TAKEN
 
3.8.2    The Committee was apprised of the following action taken by the government:-
 
The general rate of customs duty on capital goods is 15%, which is the peak rate of customs duty for non-agricultural
goods.
Customs duty on specified capital goods such as specified project imports, specified capital goods required in the
infrastructure and IT/Electronics/Telecom sectors and textile machinery not having a strong domestic angle has been
kept below 15% so as to reduce investment costs and facilitate technology upgradation/modernization.
Metals such as alloy steel, aluminum and copper, major inputs for capital goods, attract 10% customs duty. As regards
specified textile machinery attracts customs duty @ 5%, import of their parts is allowed at 5%, so as to provide level
playing field to the domestic manufacturers of such machines.
Increase in excise duty on steel should not result in increase in costs, since credit of the same would be available.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION

            The Committee notes  that the Government is extending a variety of fiscal incentives for promoting the Small
Scale Industries, however, this Committee feels that the Advisory Committee, constituted under the Chairmanship of
Member (Central Excise), Central Board of Excise and Custom (CBEC) to  advise the Government on the extent of
abatement for both excise and Service Tex, should also examine the issue of the requisite period for which such fiscal
incentive is required to promote the SSI  units. The said Advisory committee may also examine the issue of extending
the central fiscal incentives to SSI units engaged in the SSI activities to the select region of the country in such a way
that it  must ensure the balanced industrial distribution and development and prevent the shifting of the industries from
one region to another due to aberration  in the tax-incentives. ( Para : 3.1.4)
 
The Committee observes that  since the Medium enterprises are being emerging out of the SSI units and they are on the
move towards the consolidation stage, therefore, the Advisory Committee may also consider the issue of examining  as

the global pace of growth. ( Para : 3.1.5     )
